# Review of Last Class

## The Cliffhanger

Monday: forward Euler on the airshed, $\Delta t = 2.5\ \text{s}$, never settles.

$$F'(C) = 1 - l\Delta t = 1 - 0.8(2.5) = -1$$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
$|F'| = 1$ exactly: a perturbation neither grows nor decays. The simulation **oscillates forever**, undamped --- for any $l$, this happens whenever $\Delta t > 2/l$.

This is the same "does a small perturbation grow?" question you already know from CEE 3200 --- just asked about the *simulation* instead of the *system*. We won't dwell on it further; today is about a new model.
:::

# Why Dissolved Oxygen Matters

## Dissolved Oxygen

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
Dissolved oxygen (DO) is the free, non-compound oxygen present in water.

Freshwater can only hold small amounts, and this capacity is regulated by temperature.
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
![Dissolved Oxygen by temperature](https://www.fondriest.com/environmental-measurements/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/dissolvedoxygen_river-levels.jpg){width=80%}

::: {.caption}
Source: [fondriest.com](https://www.fondriest.com/environmental-measurements/parameters/water-quality/dissolved-oxygen/)
:::
:::
::::

## Dissolved Oxygen and Life

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=45%}
DO is essential for aquatic life.

**Hypoxia** occurs when DO levels are $< 2$ mg/L.
:::
::: {.column width=45%}
![Minimum DO requirements for freshwater fish](https://www.fondriest.com/environmental-measurements/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/dissolvedoxygen_levels-fresh.jpg){width=70%}

::: {.caption}
Source: [fondriest.com](https://www.fondriest.com/environmental-measurements/parameters/water-quality/dissolved-oxygen/)
:::
:::
::::

## Impact of Paris on Seine DO, 1874

![Dissolved Oxygen Downstream of Paris, 1874](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325721176/figure/fig10/AS:962439298445322@1606474818380/Longitudinal-profiles-x-axis-in-km-downstream-of-Paris-center-of-dissolved-oxygen_W640.jpg)

::: {.caption}
Source: Dmitrieva, T., et al. (2018). <https://doi.org/10.1007/s12685-018-0216-7>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
DO drops sharply below the city, then **recovers downstream**. You are about to derive exactly this shape.
:::

## DO Regulatory Standards

**Objective**: Keep DO *above* the regulatory standard.

In NY (via [Westlaw](https://govt.westlaw.com/nycrr/Document/I4ed90412cd1711dda432a117e6e0f345?viewType=FullText&originationContext=documenttoc&transitionType=CategoryPageItem&contextData=(sc.Default)&bhcp=1)):

- DO levels may not fall below 3 mg/L
- DO may not be below 4.8 mg/L for an extended period

# Deriving the Model

## Oxygen Balance in Rivers and Streams

![Processes influencing oxygen balance in moving freshwater](figures/do-processes.svg){height=100%}

## Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD)

Oxygen used by microbes during aerobic decomposition of organic matter:
$$\text{Organic Matter} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NO}_3 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{Residuals}$$

We track two kinds: **Carbonaceous BOD (CBOD)** from carbon compounds, and **Nitrogenous BOD (NBOD)** from nitrogen compounds.

## Modeling DO

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}
We track the mass balance **in terms of rates**, following an element of water as it moves downstream.
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
![Processes influencing oxygen balance in moving freshwater](figures/do-processes.svg)
:::
::::

## DO Mass Balance

Let $U$ be the river velocity (km/d), $x$ the distance downstream from a release site, and $C(x)$ the DO concentration at $x$ (mg/L):

$$U\frac{dC}{dx} = \Delta\ \text{DO} = \text{Reaeration} + \text{Photosynthesis} - \text{Respiration} - \text{Benthal Uptake} - \text{CBOD} - \text{NBOD}$$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The "clock" here is **distance downstream**, not time --- the same idea as marching in $t$, just relabeled.
:::

## BOD Oxygen Uptake

Deoxygenation from waste decomposition is first-order. In time: $M = M_0 e^{-kt}$.

Our equation is in distance, so substitute $t = x/U$:

$$B(x) = B_0 e^{-k_c x/U} \qquad\qquad N(x) = N_0 e^{-k_n x/U}$$

where $k_c$, $k_n$ are the CBOD and NBOD decay rates.

## Putting It Together

Reaeration is proportional to the deficit from saturation, $k_a(C_s - C)$. Photosynthesis ($P$), respiration ($R$), and benthal uptake ($S_B$) are usually measured and often small enough to neglect:

$$\bbox[5pt, border: 3px solid red]{U\frac{dC}{dx} = k_a(C_s - C) + P - R - S_B - k_cB_0e^{-k_cx/U} - k_nN_0e^{-k_nx/U}}$$

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
DO drops after a release, then recovers as the BOD is consumed --- the **sag curve** from the Seine data. The **minimum**, not the endpoint, is the regulated quantity.
:::

# Why Discretize an Equation You Can Already Solve?

## Analytic Solution (Streeter-Phelps)

::: {.small-math}
$$\begin{aligned}
C(x) &= C_s(1-\alpha_1) + C_0\alpha_1 - B_0\alpha_2 - N_0\alpha_3 + \left(\frac{P-R-S_B}{k_a}\right)(1-\alpha_1) \\[0.5em]
\alpha_1 &= \exp\left(\frac{-k_ax}{U}\right) \\[0.25em]
\alpha_2 &= \left(\frac{k_c}{k_a-k_c}\right)\left[\exp\left(\frac{-k_cx}{U}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-k_ax}{U}\right)\right] \\[0.25em]
\alpha_3 &= \left(\frac{k_n}{k_a-k_n}\right)\left[\exp\left(\frac{-k_nx}{U}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-k_ax}{U}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}$$
:::

## What Assumptions Did We Make?

::: {.incremental}
- $U$, $k_a$, $k_c$, $k_n$ are **constant** along the whole reach.
- $P$, $R$, $S_B$ are constant (often zero).
- A single, steady release at $x = 0$.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Every one of those is a modeling convenience, not a physical law. **What happens when they don't hold?**
:::

## Two Reasons to Discretize Anyway

::: {.quote}
> Defined more generally (analytic solution undefined when $k_a = k_c$ or $k_a = k_n$). Can add more complexity (time/temperature variation). But be careful of numerical errors and computational complexity.

::: {.cite}
--- adapted from the FA25 deck's own assessment
:::
:::

::: {.incremental}
- $\alpha_2$ and $\alpha_3$ divide by $k_a - k_c$ and $k_a - k_n$. **At $k_a = k_c$ the formula is undefined** --- a removable singularity you'd need to special-case in code. The discretized version never notices.
- The formula needs $U$, $k_a$, $k_c$, $k_n$ **constant along the reach**. That is true by assumption, not by physics: reaeration depends on temperature, which is not constant.
:::

## What Discretizing Does *Not* Buy You

Two things the closed form already handles, so don't claim them as reasons to discretize:

::: {.incremental}
- **Multiple discharges**: chain closed-form segments end to end, using one segment's output as the next segment's inlet condition. No discretization needed.
- **A constant but uncertain** $B_0$: resample it and re-evaluate the closed form as many times as you like. Still no discretization needed.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**What actually forces the issue** is a driver that is not just uncertain but genuinely **varies along the domain** --- exactly what we'll do at the end of class.
:::

## Discretizing Anyway --- One March, By Hand

$B$ and $N$ already have exact solutions, so only $C$ needs stepping:

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| output: false

# River and waste-load parameters.
ka, kc, kn = 0.6, 0.4, 0.25    # reaeration, CBOD decay, NBOD decay   [1/d]
C0, B0, N0 = 6.2, 9.0, 7.0     # initial DO deficit-state, CBOD, NBOD [mg/L]
Cs, U = 7.0, 5.0                # saturation DO [mg/L], velocity [km/d]

# Passing every rate by keyword, not position, is deliberate: the FA25
# version of this function took (ka, kn, kc) but every call site passed
# (ka, kc, kn), silently swapping the CBOD and NBOD rates. Keywords make
# that class of bug impossible.
do_change(C, x; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0) =
    (ka * (Cs - C) - kc * B0 * exp(-kc * x / U) - kn * N0 * exp(-kn * x / U)) / U

function do_march(C_ic, L, Δx; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0)
    steps = Int(round(L / Δx))
    C = zeros(steps + 1)
    C[1] = C_ic
    for i in 1:steps
        C[i+1] = C[i] + Δx * do_change(C[i], (i - 1) * Δx; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0)
    end
    return C
end
```

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This is enough to see what a solver does. **On HW3 you will solve this same model with `DifferentialEquations.jl`** --- the properly engineered version of this loop, closing the loop on Monday's unexplained `Vern9()`.
:::

## The Sag Curve

```{julia}
#| label: fig-sagcurve
#| fig-cap: "The DO sag curve: forward Euler in x against a fine reference."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

L = 40.0
p_sag = plot(xlabel="Distance downstream  [km]", ylabel="DO  [mg/L]", legend=:bottomright)
plot!(p_sag, 0:0.002:L, do_march(C0, L, 0.002; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0), color=:black,
    linewidth=5, label="reference (Δx = 0.002)")
for (Δx, col) in zip([2.0, 1.0, 0.5], [cb_vermillion, cb_orange, cb_blue])
    plot!(p_sag, 0:Δx:L, do_march(C0, L, Δx; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0), color=col,
        linewidth=3, linestyle=:dash, markershape=:circle, markersize=4, label="Δx = $Δx")
end
hline!(p_sag, [2.5], color=cb_green, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dot, label="standard: 2.5 mg/L")
plot!(p_sag, size=(1100, 450), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

::: {.caption}
The **minimum**, not the endpoint, is what a regulator checks.
:::

## Does Step Size Change the Verdict?

The standard is $2.5$ mg/L. The true minimum is $2.6$ mg/L --- this river **complies**.

| $\Delta x$ (km) | minimum DO (mg/L) | verdict |
|---:|---:|:---|
| $4.0$ | $1.3$ | **violation** ❌ |
| $2.0$ | $2.0$ | **violation** ❌ |
| $1.0$ | $2.3$ | **violation** ❌ |
| $0.5$ | $2.4$ | **violation** ❌ |
| $0.25$ | $2.5$ | complies ✓ |
| $0.125$ | $2.5$ | complies ✓ |

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Four reasonable-looking step sizes all manufacture a violation that is not there.** Sharper than Monday's airshed story: here the whole coarse-to-moderate range is wrong, not just the coarsest two.
:::

## Does It Converge at First Order?

```{julia}
#| label: fig-do-convergence
#| fig-cap: "Error in the minimum DO against step size, on log-log axes."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

Δxs = [4.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625]
min_ref = minimum(do_march(C0, L, 0.001; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0))
errs = [abs(minimum(do_march(C0, L, Δx; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, B0, N0)) - min_ref) for Δx in Δxs]
orders = [round(log2(errs[i] / errs[i+1]), digits=2) for i in 1:length(errs)-1]

p_doconv = plot(Δxs, errs, xscale=:log10, yscale=:log10, markershape=:circle,
    markersize=7, color=cb_vermillion, linewidth=3, label="forward Euler",
    xlabel="Δx  [km]", ylabel="error in minimum DO  [mg/L]", legend=:bottomright)
plot!(p_doconv, Δxs, errs[1] .* (Δxs ./ Δxs[1]), color=:black, linewidth=2,
    linestyle=:dash, label="slope 1")
plot!(p_doconv, size=(1000, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

::: {.caption}
Observed orders: `{julia} join(string.(orders), ", ")` --- the same first-order signature as Monday, on an entirely different model.
:::

# Time-Varying and Uncertain Loading

## A Load That Actually Varies

Real BOD loads vary hour to hour: a treatment plant's effluent rises and falls through the day. This is exactly the case that forces discretization --- not just uncertainty, but variation **along the domain**.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-do-timevarying
#| fig-cap: "Sag curves under five realizations of a fluctuating CBOD load."
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true

using Random
Random.seed!(4750)

function do_march_randomB(C_ic, L, Δx, B0_series; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, N0)
    steps = Int(round(L / Δx))
    C = zeros(steps + 1)
    C[1] = C_ic
    for i in 1:steps
        x = (i - 1) * Δx
        change = (ka * (Cs - C[i]) - kc * B0_series[i] * exp(-kc * x / U)
                  - kn * N0 * exp(-kn * x / U)) / U
        C[i+1] = C[i] + Δx * change
    end
    return C
end

Δx = 0.25
nsteps = Int(round(L / Δx)) + 1
p_ens = plot(xlabel="Distance downstream  [km]", ylabel="DO  [mg/L]", legend=:bottomright)
mins = Float64[]
for k in 1:5
    B0_series = B0 .* (1 .+ 0.2 .* randn(nsteps))
    Csag = do_march_randomB(C0, L, Δx, B0_series; ka, kc, kn, Cs, U, N0)
    push!(mins, minimum(Csag))
    plot!(p_ens, 0:Δx:L, Csag, color=cb_blue, alpha=0.5, linewidth=2, label=nothing)
end
hline!(p_ens, [2.5], color=cb_green, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dot, label="standard")
plot!(p_ens, size=(1000, 440), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm,
    bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm)
```

::: {.caption}
Minimum DO across 5 realizations: `{julia} join(string.(round.(mins, digits=2)), ", ")` mg/L.
:::

## How Many Runs Would We Trust?

Five realizations give five different minimum-DO values, and a real range of outcomes.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**How many runs would we need before we trust that range?**

That is not a question this lecture can answer yet --- it is a question about *sampling*, not about discretization. **Next week.**
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- The DO **sag curve** has a minimum downstream of the release --- the regulated quantity is not the endpoint.
- The closed-form Streeter-Phelps solution is undefined at $k_a = k_c$ or $k_a = k_n$, and assumes every rate is constant along the reach --- assumptions of convenience, not physics.
- Discretizing buys you **generality**, not results you couldn't already get by chaining closed-form segments or resampling a constant parameter.
- The same halve-and-check discipline from Monday applies word-for-word to $\Delta x$: four reasonable step sizes manufactured a violation that was not there.
:::
